concepts.name: More features of the Government of India Act 1935
concepts.description: Franchise, the Reserve Bank, commissions, the Federal Court, Burma, new provinces, minorities, the Railway Authority and the Auditor-General.
concepts.idea: The 1935 Act created institutions such as the RBI and the Federal Court and separated Burma from India.
concepts.rule: The 1935 Act extended the franchise so that about 14 per cent of the population could vote. It provided for a Reserve Bank of India to control currency and credit; a Federal Public Service Commission, Provincial Public Service Commissions and a Joint Public Service Commission for two or more provinces; and a Federal Court, set up in 1937. It separated Burma (Myanmar) from India and created two new provinces, Orissa and Sind. It gave safeguards for minorities, provided a Federal Railway Authority to run railways, and provided for an Auditor-General of India to audit federation and provincial accounts.
concepts.example: Orissa and Sind became provinces under the 1935 Act.

concepts.name: Background to the Indian Independence Act 1947
concepts.description: Attlee's declaration, the Mountbatten Plan of 3 June 1947 and the passage of the Act.
concepts.idea: The 1947 Act followed Attlee's announcement and the Mountbatten Plan for partition.
concepts.rule: On 20 February 1947 British Prime Minister Clement Attlee declared that British rule in India would end by 30 June 1948 with power transferred to responsible Indian hands. This was followed by Muslim League agitation demanding partition. On 3 June 1947 the British Government made it clear that any Constitution framed by the Constituent Assembly could not apply to those parts unwilling to accept it, and on the same day Lord Mountbatten, the Viceroy, put forward the partition plan, the Mountbatten Plan, which the Congress and the Muslim League accepted. The Indian Independence Bill was introduced in the British Parliament on 4 July 1947, received Royal Assent on 18 July 1947 and came into force on 15 August 1947.
concepts.example: The Indian Independence Bill was introduced in the British Parliament on 4 July 1947.

concepts.name: Features of the Independence Act 1947: dominions, Governor-General and Assemblies
concepts.description: Partition, dominion status, the end of the Viceroy's office and the powers of the two Assemblies.
concepts.idea: The Act created two dominions, abolished the Viceroy and made each Constituent Assembly sovereign.
concepts.rule: The Act ended British rule and declared India independent from 15 August 1947. It partitioned India into two independent dominions, India and Pakistan, with the right to secede from the Commonwealth. It abolished the office of Viceroy and provided a Governor-General for each dominion, appointed by the British King on the advice of the dominion cabinet; Britain had no responsibility for the governments of India or Pakistan. It empowered the Constituent Assemblies to frame any constitution and repeal any British Act, including the Independence Act itself, and to make laws for their territories till the new constitutions came into force. No British Act passed after 15 August 1947 extended to the dominions unless their legislatures extended it. It abolished the office of Secretary of State for India and transferred his functions to the Secretary of State for Commonwealth Affairs.
concepts.example: The Act allowed each dominion to leave the Commonwealth if it wished.

concepts.name: Features of the Independence Act 1947: princely states, veto and transfer of power
concepts.description: Paramountcy, the 1935 Act as interim law, the Crown's veto, nominal heads, civil services and the midnight transfer.
concepts.idea: The Act ended paramountcy, kept the 1935 Act as interim law and made the Governor-General a nominal head.
concepts.rule: The Act proclaimed the lapse of British paramountcy over the princely states and treaty relations with tribal areas from 15 August 1947, giving the states freedom to join India or Pakistan or remain independent. Until the new constitutions, each dominion and its provinces were governed by the 1935 Act, which they could modify. The British monarch lost the right to veto bills or reserve them for approval; this right was reserved for the Governor-General, who could assent in the name of His Majesty. The Governor-General and the provincial governors became constitutional (nominal) heads acting on the advice of their councils of ministers. The title of Emperor of India was dropped from the King's titles. Appointments and reservations of posts in civil services by the Secretary of State ended, though earlier appointees kept their benefits. At midnight on 14-15 August 1947 British rule ended; Mountbatten became the first Governor-General of the Dominion of India and swore in Nehru as first Prime Minister, and the Constituent Assembly became the dominion Parliament. The boundary between the dominions was fixed by a Boundary Commission headed by Radcliffe; Pakistan included West Punjab, Sind, Baluchistan, East Bengal, the North-Western Frontier Province and the Sylhet district of Assam, the last two by referendum.
concepts.example: Radcliffe headed the Boundary Commission that fixed the border between India and Pakistan.

concepts.name: Beginnings of British rule and background facts from the notes
concepts.description: The Company's beginnings, the Diwani, the Crown takeover and points from the footnotes on services, budget and reform declarations.
concepts.idea: The Company began as a trader in 1608, gained the Diwani in 1765 and gave way to the Crown in 1858.
concepts.rule: The British came to India in 1608 as traders of the East India Company, which had an exclusive trading right under a charter of Queen Elizabeth I in 1600. In 1765 the Company obtained the Diwani, rights over revenue and civil justice of Bengal, Bihar and Orissa, granted by the Mughal Emperor Shah Alam after the Battle of Buxar (1764). In 1858, after the sepoy mutiny, the Crown took direct responsibility; British rule lasted until 15 August 1947. The Constituent Assembly was formed in 1946 and the Constitution came into being on 26 January 1950. Pitt's India Act was introduced by Prime Minister William Pitt. The covenanted civil service was the higher service and the uncovenanted the lower. The Budget system began in British India in 1860. The 1917 declaration (20 August 1917) spoke of increasing association of Indians and gradual development of self-governing institutions towards responsible government. A Public Service Commission was set up in 1926 on the Lee Commission's recommendation (1923-24).
concepts.example: The Company obtained the Diwani of Bengal, Bihar and Orissa in 1765.
